title: Spectral signatures of spin textures and the emergence of a pseudogap
authors: Matteo Quinzi, Andrea Pintus, Tommaso Chiarotti, Massimo Capone, Nicola Marzari
abstract: Periodic solids with strongly interacting electrons display phenomena -- from Mott localization to high-temperature superconductivity -- that escape conventional band theory. Efforts to address this unconventional physics have been typically cast in the language of Green's function theories and the associated frequency- and momentum-dependent self-energies capturing strong correlations beyond the reach of mean-field theories. Here, we underscore that frequency- and momentum-dependent self-energies emerge also from mean-field solutions that break translational symmetry, and that these self-energies can display the characteristic fingerprints of strong correlations for certain, physically meaningful, spatial patterns. We showcase this perspective by studying the paradigmatic case of the 2D Hubbard model. We find that already at the mean-field level the doped antiferromagnet displays, in addition to stripes, many quasi-degenerate self-consistent solutions with antiferromagnetic textures organized into antiphase domains separated by hole-rich interfaces, reminiscent of the phase-separation scenario. Remarkably, these solutions map into spectral functions that display very distinctively the phenomenology of the pseudogap, including the nodal-antinodal dichotomy of the self-energy, Fermi arcs, and a complementary Luttinger surface. The result is a conceptually simple description of such an intricate many-body state: the pseudogap emerges as the momentum-space spectral portrait of the real-space interplay between antiferromagnetic domains and the metallic interfaces, which echoes the role of spin-fluctuations identified by nonperturbative methods.
summary: This work investigates how strong correlations manifest in the 2D Hubbard model by analyzing spin textures (STs) in the mean-field limit. The authors demonstrate that the characteristic pseudogap spectral signature arises not from long-range order, but from the momentum-space averaging of the real-space interplay between antiferromagnetic domains and metallic interfaces. This provides a novel, conceptually simple description of complex many-body physics.
main_problem: Understanding exotic phenomena in strongly interacting periodic solids, such as high-temperature superconductivity, which defy conventional band theory.
main_result: The pseudogap phenomenology, including nodal-antinodal dichotomy and Fermi arcs, emerges naturally as the momentum-space spectral portrait resulting from the real-space interplay between antiferromagnetic domains and metallic interfaces.
method: The study employs Green's function theories, analyzing mean-field solutions that break translational symmetry to derive frequency- and momentum-dependent self-energies.
model_or_system: The primary model studied is the 2D Hubbard model, focusing on the physics of a hole-doped antiferromagnet.
key_observables: Self-energy $\Sigma(\mathbf{k}, \omega)$, spectral functions, nodal-antinodal dichotomy, Fermi arcs, Luttinger surface, Néel parameter ($\Delta_r$), and hole density ($h_r$).
important_parameters: Hole doping ($p$), interaction strength ($U$), and second-neighbor hopping ($t'$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on mean-field approximations (e.g., Hartree-Fock) and uses an ensemble average over quasi-degenerate spin texture solutions to approximate the true many-body state.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the real-space spin textures (antiphase domains), the resulting spectral functions showing the pseudogap, and the evolution of these features as parameters like doping or hopping are varied.
paper_structure: The paper develops the concept by first establishing that mean-field self-energies can capture strong correlation fingerprints. It then applies this to the 2D Hubbard model, showing how the real-space structure of spin textures dictates the momentum-space spectral signature of the pseudogap.
why_interesting: The explicit derivation of complex many-body spectral features (like the pseudogap) from a relatively simple mean-field description of real-space magnetic textures offers a conceptually simple, yet powerful, theoretical framework for understanding high-Tc superconductivity.
